questions.question: In your Web Chess Application, you implemented real-time chess piece detection using a webcam and OpenCV. Can you describe how you integrated the video stream into the web page and how the detection results were displayed to the user?
You mentioned using YOLO and CNN models achieving 86% training accuracy. What factors did you consider when choosing YOLO over other object detection architectures for this project?

During your role at GenVision Technologies, you built UI features with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Can you give an example of a component you created and the specific JavaScript techniques you used to make it interactive?
Explain the concept of event delegation in JavaScript and why it can be beneficial for dynamic UI elements.
What strategies would you employ to reduce the initial load time of a single-page application that includes heavy media assets, such as the webcam feed used in your chess project?

2.answer_text:
I picked YOLO specifically for the chess project's piece detection — not the crop disease one (that's a plain CNN classifier, no object detection needed there since it's whole-leaf-image classification).

For the chess piece detection: I chose YOLO over other architectures (like Faster R-CNN or SSD) mainly because it's a single-pass detector — fast enough for real-time inference on a live webcam feed, which two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN aren't well-suited for. It also has strong tooling support via Roboflow for labeling and training, which fit my dataset size (~400 labeled images) and timeline. Accuracy-wise, YOLO handles small, densely-packed objects reasonably well, which matters on a chessboard where multiple pieces sit close together.

3.answer_text: At GenVision, I built a dynamic form validation component — as the user typed into input fields, I used JavaScript event listeners (input and blur events) to validate data in real-time and show inline error messages without a page reload. I also used DOM manipulation to toggle CSS classes for error/success states, and debounced the input events so validation didn't fire on every keystroke, which kept it smooth.

5.answer_text:
For a single-page application with a webcam feed, I would focus on these strategies:

Code splitting – Load only the JavaScript required for the initial page. Load chess logic, OpenCV/model code, etc. only when the user enters that feature.
Lazy-load heavy components – Don't initialize the webcam immediately. Start getUserMedia() only when the user opens the camera/chess detection screen.
Optimize webcam resolution/FPS – Use a reasonable camera constraint such as 1280×720 or even lower if the model doesn't need high resolution. Lower frame rates can also reduce processing and bandwidth.
Lazy-load images/videos – Non-critical media should not be downloaded during the initial page load. For videos, preload="none" can prevent unnecessary downloads.
Compress media – Use efficient formats such as WebP/AVIF for images and appropriately compressed video. Heavy media can represent a large portion of the bytes downloaded by a website.
Defer ML model loading – If your chess project uses a YOLO/model for piece detection, don't load the model during initial page rendering. Load it when the user actually starts chess recognition.
Cache static assets – Use browser caching/CDN caching for JavaScript bundles, images, CSS, and model files so repeat visits don't require downloading everything again.
Measure with Lighthouse/DevTools – Check the network waterfall and identify which resources are delaying the first meaningful render/LCP.
